claim: CAMTAs are a highly conserved family of CaM-binding transcription activators.
source: Calmodulin-binding transcription activators (CAMTAs) are a highly conserved family of CaM-binding transcription activators (Finkler et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finkler et al., 2007

claim: In plants, CAMTAs mediate transcriptional changes in response to Ca2+ signals evoked by biotic and abiotic stress.
source: In plants, CAMTAs mediate transcriptional changes in response to Ca2+ signals evoked by biotic and abiotic stress (Yang and Poovaiah, 2002; Du et al., 2009; Doherty et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2013; Shkolnik et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work

claim: Mammals encode two CAMTA proteins, CAMTA1 and CAMTA2, respectively enriched in the brain and heart.
source: Mammals encode two CAMTA proteins, CAMTA1 and CAMTA2, respectively enriched in the brain and heart (Song et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2006

claim: Loss of CAMTA1 in the mouse nervous system leads to defects in hippocampal-dependent memory formation, degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and ataxia.
source: Loss of CAMTA1 in the mouse nervous system leads to defects in hippocampal-dependent memory formation, degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and ataxia (Long et al., 2014; Bas-Orth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Long et al., 2014 and Bas-Orth et al., 2016

claim: Humans heterozygous for lesions in the CAMTA1 gene exhibit a range of neurological phenotypes, including intellectual disability, cerebellar ataxia, and reduced memory performance.
source: Humans heterozygous for lesions in the CAMTA1 gene exhibit a range of neurological phenotypes, including intellectual disability, cerebellar ataxia, and reduced memory performance (Huentelman et al., 2007; Thevenon et al., 2012; Shinawi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: CaM is a ubiquitously expressed Ca2+ binding protein that plays a key role in transducing responses to Ca2+ changes.
source: CaM is a ubiquitously expressed Ca2+ binding protein that plays a key role in transducing responses to Ca2+ changes (Faas et al., 2011; Baimbridge et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Faas et al., 2011 and Baimbridge et al., 1992

claim: Ca2+-CaM modifies a host of neuronal functions, including signal transduction, ion currents, vesicle fusion, learning and memory, metabolism, and apoptosis.
source: Ca2+-CaM modifies a host of neuronal functions, including signal transduction, ion currents, vesicle fusion, learning and memory, metabolism, and apoptosis (Hoeflich and Ikura, 2002; Berchtold and Villalobo, 2014), by regulating dozens of binding targets including the CaM kinases, calcineurin, and diverse ion channels (Wayman et al., 2008; Saimi and Kung, 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: CaM levels are thought to be limiting compared to the combined concentration of Ca2+-CaM binding proteins.
source: CaM levels are thought to be limiting compared to the combined concentration of Ca2+-CaM binding proteins (Sanabria et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanabria et al., 2008

claim: Relatively small changes in CaM levels are predicted to impact Ca2+-CaM regulation of downstream targets.
source: relatively small changes in CaM levels are predicted to impact Ca2+-CaM regulation of downstream targets (Pepke et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pepke et al., 2010

claim: Most natural isolates of C. elegans feed in groups.
source: Most natural isolates of C. elegans feed in groups.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The standard C. elegans lab strain, N2, feeds alone, due to a gain-of-function mutation in a neuropeptide receptor called NPR-1.
source: By contrast, the standard C. elegans lab strain, N2, feeds alone, due to a gain-of-function mutation in a neuropeptide receptor called NPR-1 (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Bono and Bargmann, 1998

claim: npr-1(ad609) null mutants aggregate strongly.
source: Using npr-1(ad609) null mutants of the N2 strain (denoted as npr-1 throughout this manuscript), which aggregate strongly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: A forward genetic screen for genes required for aggregation identified multiple aggregation-defective strains with mutations in camt-1, the sole C. elegans CAMTA.
source: we performed a forward genetic screen for genes required for aggregation (Chen et al., 2017). The screen identified multiple aggregation-defective strains with mutations in camt-1, the sole C. elegans CAMTA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from genetic screen and reference to figure

claim: Aggregation is closely linked to escape from normoxia (21% O2).
source: Aggregation is closely linked to escape from normoxia (21% O2) (Busch et al., 2012; Rogers et al., 2006; Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Normoxia elicits rapid movement in npr-1 animals, which is rapidly suppressed when O2 levels drop.
source: Normoxia elicits rapid movement in npr-1 animals, which is rapidly suppressed when O2 levels drop (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: camt-1 mutants showed defective responses to O2 stimuli.
source: camt-1 mutants showed defective responses to O2 stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: camt-1(db973); npr-1 animals were hyperactive in 7% O2, and showed reduced arousal when switched from 7% to 21% O2.
source: Compared to npr-1 controls, animals from a mutant strain isolated in the screen, camt-1(db973); npr-1, which harbors a premature stop codon in CAMT-1 (Q222*), were hyperactive in 7% O2, and showed reduced arousal when switched from 7% to 21% O2 (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B

claim: camt-1(ok515) deletion conferred similar defects to camt-1(db973).
source: A deletion (The C. elegans Deletion Mutant Consortium, 2012) that removed 451 residues of CAMT-1, camt-1(ok515), conferred similar defects (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B

claim: A fosmid transgene containing a wild-type copy of the camt-1 genomic locus rescued camt-1 mutant phenotypes.
source: A fosmid transgene containing a wild-type (WT) copy of the camt-1 genomic locus rescued camt-1 mutant phenotypes, restoring fast movement at 21% O2, and slow movement at 7% O2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: CAMT-1 is required for C. elegans to respond appropriately to different O2 levels.
source: These results indicate that CAMT-1 is required for C. elegans to respond appropriately to different O2 levels.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments and mutant phenotypes

claim: CAMT-1 has the characteristic domain architecture of CAMTAs: a DNA-binding domain (CG-1), an immunoglobulin-like fold (IPT/TIG), ankyrin repeats (ANKs), a putative Ca2+-dependent CaM-binding domain (CaMBD) and multiple IQ motifs.
source: CAMT-1 has the characteristic domain architecture of CAMTAs (Finkler et al., 2007): a DNA-binding domain (CG-1), an immunoglobulin-like fold (IPT/TIG) similar to those found in non-specific DNA-binding/dimerization domains of other transcription factors, ankyrin repeats (ANKs), a putative Ca2+-dependent CaM-binding domain (CaMBD) and multiple IQ motifs that are thought to bind CaM in a Ca2+-independent manner (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C; Bouché et al., 2002; Choi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations and shown in figures

claim: CAMT-1 has predicted nuclear localization and nuclear export signals (NLS/NES).
source: CAMT-1 also has predicted nuclear localization and nuclear export signals (NLS/NES, Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on computational prediction shown in Figure 1B

claim: In mice, humans, and flies, CAMTA transcription factors are expressed in many brain regions.
source: In mice, humans, and flies, CAMTA transcription factors are expressed in many brain regions (Huentelman et al., 2007; Bas-Orth et al., 2016; Sato et al., 2019; Long et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: CAMT-1 is expressed broadly and specifically in the nervous system.
source: This fluorescent reporter was functional, as it rescued the behavioral defects of camt-1 mutants (Figure 1C), and revealed that CAMT-1 was expressed broadly and specifically in the nervous system (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: CAMT-1 is expressed in sensory neurons with exposed ciliated endings, motor neurons of the ventral cord, the URX O2-sensing neuron, and the RMG hub interneurons.
source: We observed CAMT-1 expression in sensory neurons with exposed ciliated endings, motor neurons of the ventral cord, the URX O2-sensing neuron, and URX's post-synaptic partner, the RMG hub interneurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: camt-1 mutants exhibited abnormally high levels of Ω-turns without a CO2 stimulus and a prolonged increase in Ω-turns in response to a rise in CO2.
source: camt-1 mutants exhibited abnormally high levels of Ω-turns without a CO2 stimulus and a prolonged increase in Ω-turns in response to a rise in CO2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Chemotaxis toward NaCl and odorant attractants such as benzaldehyde and diacetyl was reduced in camt-1 mutants.
source: Chemotaxis toward NaCl and odorant attractants such as benzaldehyde and diacetyl was reduced in camt-1 mutants, and these defects were rescued by a fosmid transgene containing WT CAMT-1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: CAMT-1 function is important for multiple C. elegans behaviors.
source: Taken together, these data show that CAMT-1 function is important for multiple C. elegans behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple behavioral defects observed in camt-1 mutants

claim: Many deleterious human alleles of CAMTA1 alter the CG-1 DNA-binding domain.
source: Many deleterious human alleles of CAMTA1 alter the CG-1 DNA-binding domain (Thevenon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thevenon et al., 2012

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 engineered mutations in conserved residues of the CG-1 domain showed defects in aggregation and in their response to O2.
source: To assess the importance of the putative DNA-binding domain of CAMT-1, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to engineer mutations in conserved residues of the CG-1 domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). These mutants showed defects in aggregation and in their response to O2, recapitulating phenotypes of the camt-1 deletion mutants described above (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: CAMT-1 binding to DNA is essential for its function, at least for O2 escape behavior.
source: These results suggest that CAMT-1 binding to DNA is essential for its function, at least for O2 escape behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotypes of CG-1 domain mutants

claim: O2 is sensed mainly by the sensory neurons URX, AQR, and PQR.
source: O2 is sensed mainly by the sensory neurons URX, AQR, and PQR, and tonic signaling from URX to RMG drives high locomotory activity at 21% O2 (Busch et al., 2012; Zimmer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Busch et al., 2012 and Zimmer et al., 2009

claim: Selectively expressing CAMT-1 to the RMG hub interneurons, but not O2 sensing neurons, rescued the fast movement at 21% O2 of camt-1 mutants.
source: Selectively expressing CAMT-1 to the RMG hub interneurons, but not O2 sensing neurons, rescued the fast movement at 21% O2 of camt-1 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E

claim: The defective response of camt-1 mutants to 7% O2 was not rescued by expressing CAMT-1 in RMG, or by simultaneous expression in RMG and O2-sensing neurons.
source: The defective response of camt-1 mutants to 7% O2 was not rescued by expressing CAMT-1 in RMG, or by simultaneous expression in RMG and O2-sensing neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E

claim: CAMT-1 acts in multiple neurons.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which CAMT-1 acts in multiple neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the cell-specific rescue experiments

claim: Pan-neuronal expression rescued camt-1 mutant phenotypes, and expression of the isoform a alone (CAMT-1a) was sufficient for rescue.
source: As expected, pan-neuronal expression rescued camt-1 mutant phenotypes, and expression of the isoform a alone (CAMT-1a) was sufficient for rescue (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Ca2+-CaM dependent changes in gene expression are known to be important for both the development and function of the nervous system.
source: Ca2+-CaM dependent changes in gene expression are known to be important for both the development and function of the nervous system (West et al., 2002; Chin and Means, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to West et al., 2002 and Chin and Means, 2000

claim: Inducing CAMT-1 expression in the last larval stage/young adults rescued the aggregation and speed response defects, albeit not completely.
source: By contrast, inducing CAMT-1 expression in the last larval stage/young adults rescued the aggregation (data not shown) and speed response defects, albeit not completely (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: CAMT-1 can function in adults post-developmentally to regulate behavioral responses to ambient O2.
source: suggesting that CAMT-1 can function in adults post-developmentally to regulate behavioral responses to ambient O2.
evidence: Inferred from the heat-shock rescue experiments

claim: Baseline Ca2+ and stimulus-evoked Ca2+ responses in URX, BAG, and AFD neurons were significantly elevated in camt-1 mutants across all the O2/CO2 conditions tested.
source: We found that baseline Ca2+ and stimulus-evoked Ca2+ responses in URX, BAG, and AFD neurons were significantly elevated in camt-1 mutants across all the O2/CO2 conditions we tested (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: CAMT-1 activity dampens the Ca2+ responses of sensory neurons.
source: These data suggest that CAMT-1 activity somehow dampens the Ca2+ responses of these sensory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the elevated Ca2+ responses in camt-1 mutants

claim: Overexpressing CAMT-1 cDNA specifically in O2 sensors or in BAG neurons reduced Ca2+ baselines and responses.
source: We observed the converse phenotype, reduced Ca2+ baselines and responses, when we overexpressed CAMT-1 cDNA specifically in O2 sensors or in BAG neurons of control animals (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: camt-1 regulates the excitability of sensory neurons.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that camt-1 regulates the excitability of sensory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the Ca2+ imaging experiments

claim: cmd-1 (calmodulin-1) was one of only two genes whose expression was reduced in all four neural profiles relative to WT controls.
source: A striking exception was cmd-1 (calmodulin-1), encoding C. elegans CaM. cmd-1 was one of only two genes whose expression was reduced in all four neural profiles relative to WT controls.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Y41C4A.17 has no known homolog in mammals.
source: The other gene, Y41C4A.17, has no known homolog in mammals.
evidence: Based on sequence homology analysis

claim: Most of the gene expression changes in URX/AQR/PQR neurons in camt-1 mutants are due to altered Ca2+ signaling rather than direct control by CAMT-1.
source: These results support the hypothesis that most of the genes expression changes we observe in O2 sensing neurons in camt-1 mutants are due to altered Ca2+ signaling rather than direct control by CAMT-1, but that cmd-1, encoding CaM, is an exception.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of gene expression in different genetic backgrounds

claim: The levels of CaM mRNA in camt-1 mutants was 2.5- to 4-fold lower than in controls, depending on neural type.
source: The levels of CaM mRNA in camt-1 mutants was 2.5- to 4-fold lower than in controls, depending on neural type (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Disrupting cmd-1 confers lethality.
source: Straightforward comparison of camt-1 and cmd-1 loss of function phenotypes was not possible, since disrupting cmd-1 confers lethality (Karabinos et al., 2003; Au et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karabinos et al., 2003 and Au et al., 2019

claim: Supplementing CMD-1/CaM expression in camt-1 mutants using a pan-neuronal promoter rescued camt-1 phenotypes.
source: We therefore, asked if supplementing CMD-1/CaM expression in camt-1 mutants, using a pan-neuronal promoter (rab-3p), could rescue camt-1 phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in subsequent figures

claim: The rab-3p::cmd-1::SL2::mCherry transgene expressing the lowest levels of fluorescence strongly rescued the abnormal O2-escape response of camt-1 mutants.
source: The rab-3p::cmd-1::SL2::mCherry transgene expressing the lowest levels of fluorescence (line A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) strongly rescued the abnormal O2-escape response of camt-1 mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Supplementing CMD-1 in the nervous system restored normal chemotaxis toward salt, benzaldehyde, and diacetyl in camt-1 mutants.
source: Supplementing CMD-1 in the nervous system using the lowest expressing rab-3p::cmd-1::SL2::mCherry line also restored normal chemotaxis toward salt, benzaldehyde, and diacetyl in camt-1 mutants (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Supplementing CMD-1 in the nervous system rescued the hyperexcitability defects in URX and BAG neurons of camt-1 mutants.
source: and rescued the hyperexcitability defects in URX and BAG neurons of camt-1 mutants (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F-G

claim: Deleting the entire coding region of Y41C4A.17 did not affect aggregation of npr-1 animals.
source: By contrast, deleting the entire coding region of Y41C4A.17 did not affect aggregation of npr-1 animals (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown)

claim: Reduced CMD-1 expression accounts for camt-1 Ca2+ signaling and behavioral defects.
source: Our data suggest that reduced CMD-1 expression accounts for camt-1 Ca2+ signaling and behavioral defects (see also below).
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments with CMD-1

claim: Fly mutants of CAMTA show slow termination of photoresponses compared to WT controls.
source: Fly mutants of CAMTA show slow termination of photoresponses compared to WT controls (Han et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2006

claim: Fly mutants of CAMTA exhibit defects in male courtship song.
source: and also exhibit defects in male courtship song (Sato et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sato et al., 2019

claim: An allele of the Drosophila CaM gene that deletes part of the promoter and reduces CaM expression shows slow termination of photoresponses.
source: An allele of the Drosophila CaM gene that deletes part of the promoter and reduces CaM expression also shows slow termination of photoresponses (Scott et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scott et al., 1997

claim: tes2 mutants showed a modest decrease in dCAMTA mRNA level.
source: tes2 mutants showed a modest decrease in dCAMTA mRNA level, suggesting that the premature stop late in the protein does not induce mRNA degradation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The level of dCAMTA mRNA was strongly reduced in cro mutants.
source: The level of dCAMTA mRNA was strongly reduced in cro mutants as reported previously (Sato et al., 2019; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Both tes2 and cro mutant flies showed significant decreases in CaM expression compared to controls.
source: Each method reported significant decreases in CaM expression compared to controls in both tes2 and cro mutant flies (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: Immunostaining dissected retinas from cro mutants showed reduced CaM expression in rhabdomeres.
source: Moreover, immunostaining dissected retinas from cro mutants showed reduced CaM expression in rhabdomeres (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E

claim: The transcriptional upregulation of neuronal CaM by CAMTA is conserved from worms to flies.
source: These results suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of neuronal CaM by CAMTA is conserved from worms to flies.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results in both C. elegans and Drosophila

claim: ChIP-seq analysis revealed about 200 loci that were significantly enriched in CAMT-1a::GFP pulldowns compared to input and to a mock pulldown.
source: Our analysis revealed about 200 loci that were significantly enriched in CAMT-1a::GFP pulldowns compared to input, and to a mock pulldown (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq experimental data

claim: cmd-1 was at the top of the list of loci enriched in CAMT-1a::GFP pulldowns.
source: At the top of the list was cmd-1: we observed three peaks at ~6.3 kb, 4.8 kb, and 2.2 kb upstream of the CMD-1 translation start site in the CAMT-1a::GFP pulldown experiments (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: CAMT-1 is recruited to multiple sites upstream of cmd-1.
source: Thus, CAMT-1 is recruited to multiple sites upstream of cmd-1.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-seq peaks observed

claim: A CAMT-1 binding peak was found in the promoter region of Y41C4A.17.
source: A CAMT-1 binding peak was also found in the promoter region of Y41C4A.17, the only other gene whose expression was reduced in all the neurons profiled from camt-1 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: A strain harboring all three deletions at CAMT-1 ChIP-seq peaks (db1278) exhibited strong aggregation defects and defects in the locomotory responses to O2 that mirrored those of camt-1 loss-of-function mutants.
source: However, a strain harboring all three deletions (Figure 6A–B, db1278) exhibited strong aggregation defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and defects in the locomotory responses to O2 that mirrored those of camt-1 loss-of-function mutants (Figure 6B, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures

claim: The hyperactivity at 7% O2 of db1278 mutants could be rescued by expressing additional CMD-1 in the nervous system.
source: Notably, the hyperactivity at 7% O2 of db1278 mutants could be rescued by expressing additional CMD-1 in the nervous system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: cmd-1(db1278) mutants showed chemotaxis defects toward salt, benzaldehyde, and diacetyl that could be rescued by supplementing neuronal expression of CMD-1.
source: Like camt-1(ok515) mutants, cmd-1(db1278) mutants also showed chemotaxis defects toward salt, benzaldehyde, and diacetyl that could be rescued by supplementing neuronal expression of CMD-1 (compare Figures 4D and 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 6C

claim: CAMT-1 binds multiple sites in the CMD-1 promoter and acts redundantly at these sites to promote neuronal CaM expression.
source: These results suggest that CAMT-1 binds multiple sites in the CMD-1 promoter and acts redundantly at these sites to promote neuronal CaM expression.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-seq and deletion mutant experiments

claim: Animals expressing rab-3p::cmd-1 reduced neuronal expression of GFP from the cmd-1p::gfp reporter.
source: Animals expressing rab-3p::cmd-1 reduced neuronal expression of GFP from the cmd-1p::gfp reporter.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: High levels of CMD-1 can repress expression from the cmd-1 promoter.
source: These data suggest that the high levels of CMD-1 can repress expression from the cmd-1 promoter (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the reporter expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: The camt-1(4IQ*) allele did not disrupt the O2-avoidance behaviors of npr-1 mutant animals.
source: The camt-1(4IQ*) allele did not disrupt the O2-avoidance behaviors of npr-1 mutant animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: CaM binding to CAMT-1 via the IQ motifs is not essential for O2 escape behavior.
source: suggesting that CaM binding to CAMT-1 via the IQ motifs is not essential for O2 escape behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of phenotype in camt-1(4IQ*) mutants

claim: camt-1(4IQ*) animals expressing cmd-1p::gfp and rab-3p::cmd-1 showed neuronal GFP levels similar to those found in control animals lacking the rab-3p::cmd-1 transgene.
source: By contrast, we found that camt-1(4IQ*) animals expressing cmd-1p::gfp and rab-3p::cmd-1 showed neuronal GFP levels similar to those found in control animals lacking the rab-3p::cmd-1 transgene (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: CMD-1/CaM can negatively regulate its own expression by binding the IQ domains of CAMT-1.
source: These data suggest that CMD-1/CaM can negatively regulate its own expression by binding the IQ domains of CAMT-1.
evidence: Inferred from the reporter expression experiments with IQ mutants

claim: CAMT-1 may not only activate cmd-1 expression, but also repress it when available CMD-1/CaM levels are high.
source: Thus, CAMT-1 may not only activate cmd-1 expression, but also repress it when available CMD-1/CaM levels are high (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the negative feedback experiments

claim: CAMTA is a key regulator of CaM expression in multiple neuron types in both C. elegans and Drosophila.
source: We identify CAMTA as a key regulator of CaM expression in multiple neuron types, and in both Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both organisms

claim: CAMTA is a general and conserved regulator of Ca2+/CaM signaling in nervous systems.
source: and suggest that it is a general and conserved regulator of Ca2+/CaM signaling in nervous systems.
evidence: Inferred from the data across multiple species and neuron types

claim: Reduced CaM levels appear to explain the pleiotropic phenotypes of C. elegans camt-1 mutants.
source: Reduced CaM levels appear to explain the pleiotropic phenotypes of C. elegans camt-1 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments with CaM

claim: camt-1 phenotypes can be rescued by supplementing neurons with CaM.
source: First, camt-1 phenotypes can be rescued by supplementing neurons with CaM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Deleting CAMT-1 binding sites in the CaM promotor phenocopies camt-1.
source: Second, deleting CAMT-1 binding sites in the CaM promotor phenocopies camt-1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: CAMT-1 stimulates CaM expression in each of the four neurons profiled.
source: Profiling four different C. elegans neurons from camt-1 mutants and WT controls using FAC sorting and RNA Seq shows that CAMT-1 stimulates CaM expression in each of the four neurons.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data

claim: CAMT-1 is part of a general mechanism that regulates CaM levels throughout the nervous system.
source: These results, together with the observation that CAMT-1 is expressed in most or all C. elegans neurons, suggest that CAMT-1 is part of a general mechanism that regulates CaM levels throughout the nervous system.
evidence: Inferred from the expression pattern and RNA-seq data

claim: The RNA Seq experiments reveal a 2.5×–4× reduction in CaM mRNA levels in camt-1 mutants, depending on neuron type.
source: The RNA Seq experiments reveal a 2.5×–4× reduction in CaM mRNA levels in camt-1 mutants, depending on neuron type.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data

claim: These relatively small decreases in CaM mRNA are associated with striking alterations in the stimulus-evoked Ca2+ responses of each neuron.
source: These relatively small decreases in CaM mRNA are, however, associated with striking alterations in the stimulus-evoked Ca2+ responses of each neuron.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data

claim: Neural function is sensitive to quite small changes in CaM transcription.
source: These findings suggest neural function is sensitive to quite small changes in CaM transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between CaM mRNA levels and Ca2+ responses

claim: CaM levels may provide a sensitive point of regulation of neural physiology.
source: CaM levels may therefore provide a sensitive point of regulation of neural physiology.
evidence: Speculative inference from the data

claim: Previous work has identified multiple Ca2+-CaM feedback loops regulating C. elegans sensory responses, mediated by calcineurin/TAX-6, CaM kinase I/CMK-1, and PDE1/PDE-1.
source: Previous work has identified multiple Ca2+-CaM feedback loops regulating C. elegans sensory responses, mediated for example by calcineurin/TAX-6 (Kuhara et al., 2002), CaM kinase I/CMK-1 (Satterlee et al., 2004), and PDE1/PDE-1 (Couto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Work in vertebrates has shown that CaM regulates the activity of cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels and the L-type–Ca2+ channel.
source: In addition, work in vertebrates (Saimi and Kung, 2002) has shown that CaM regulates the activity of cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels and the L-type–Ca2+ channel, which contribute to the Ca2+ responses of these C. elegans sensory neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Saimi and Kung, 2002

claim: Most gene expression changes in O2 sensors in camt-1 mutants are linked to increased Ca2+ levels rather than loss of CAMT-1 per se.
source: Our analysis of mutants that abolish O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in these neurons shows that most of these expression changes are linked to increased Ca2+ levels in camt-1 mutants, rather than loss of CAMT-1 per se.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from different genetic backgrounds

claim: This is consistent with the known role of Ca2+ in regulating neuronal transcription.
source: This is consistent with the known role of Ca2+ in regulating neuronal transcription (Yap and Greenberg, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yap and Greenberg, 2018

claim: ChIP-seq studies identified CMD-1 as one of the major direct targets of CAMT-1.
source: Our ChIP-seq studies identified CMD-1 as one of the major direct targets of CAMT-1.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data

claim: There are four mouse CAMTA1 binding motifs overlapping with the CAMT-1 binding peaks of the cmd-1 promoter.
source: we note that there are four mouse CAMTA1 binding motifs (Long et al., 2014; Long et al., 2009) overlapping with the CAMT-1 binding peaks of the cmd-1 promoter.
evidence: Supported by citations to Long et al., 2014 and Long et al., 2009

claim: Mutations in the sole Drosophila CAMTA, dCAMTA, cause an approximately two fold reduction in CaM mRNA and protein in the Drosophila head.
source: Mutations in the sole Drosophila CAMTA, dCAMTA, cause an approximately two fold reduction in CaM mRNA and protein in the Drosophila head.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The regulation of CaM expression by CAMTA proteins is conserved across phylogeny.
source: These results suggest that the regulation of CaM expression by CAMTA proteins is conserved across phylogeny.
evidence: Inferred from data in multiple species

claim: In Arabidopsis, CAMTA3/AtSR1 binds in vitro to the promoter of CaM2.
source: Conservation may extend beyond metazoa, as in Arabidopsis, CAMTA3/AtSR1 binds in vitro to the promoter of CaM2, although whether this regulates CaM2 expression in vivo is unknown (Yang and Poovaiah, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang and Poovaiah, 2002

claim: dCAMTA is expressed broadly in the nervous system.
source: Like CAMT-1, dCAMTA is expressed broadly in the nervous system (Sato et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sato et al., 2019

claim: dCAMTA mutants have defective termination of photoresponses.
source: Previous work found that dCAMTA mutants have defective termination of photoresponses (Han et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2006

claim: A promoter mutation in the fly CaM gene that reduces CaM expression disrupts photoresponse termination in Drosophila photoreceptors.
source: A separate study showed that a promoter mutation in the fly CaM gene that reduces CaM expression also disrupts photoresponse termination in Drosophila photoreceptors (Scott et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scott et al., 1997

claim: dCAMTA mutants show reduced levels of CaM in photoreceptors.
source: Since dCAMTA mutants show reduced levels of CaM in photoreceptors (although not to the same extent as the promoter mutation)
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Part of the photoresponse termination defect in dCAMTA mutants may reflect reduced levels of CaM.
source: part of the photoresponse termination defect in these animals may reflect reduced levels of CaM.
evidence: Speculative inference from the data

claim: CAMTA1 is expressed broadly in both the mouse and human nervous systems.
source: CAMTA1 is expressed broadly in both the mouse and human nervous systems.
evidence: Based on established knowledge

claim: Homozygous mice and heterozygous human patients bearing mutations in CAMTA1 exhibit pleiotropic behavioral phenotypes, including memory defects and neurodegeneration.
source: Homozygous mice and heterozygous human patients bearing mutations in CAMTA1 exhibit pleiotropic behavioral phenotypes, including memory defects and neurodegeneration (Han et al., 2006; Sato et al., 2019; Long et al., 2014; Bas-Orth et al., 2016; Thevenon et al., 2012; Huentelman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The behavioral defects in CAMTA1 mutants may be functionally associated with a reduction in CaM expression.
source: Our work raises the possibility that these defects are functionally associated with a reduction in CaM expression (Zalcman et al., 2018; Wayman et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citations

claim: CAMTA2 is expressed in cardiomyocytes, and is implicated in promoting cardiac growth.
source: CAMTA2 is expressed in cardiomyocytes, and is implicated in promoting cardiac growth: overexpressing CAMTA2 in the mouse heart leads to cardiac hypertrophy (Song et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2006

claim: Selectively overexpressing CaM in the mouse heart induces cardiac hypertrophy, by a calcineurin-dependent mechanism.
source: Selectively overexpressing CaM in the mouse heart also induces cardiac hypertrophy, by a calcineurin-dependent mechanism (Obata et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Obata et al., 2005

claim: CAMTAs have been shown to mediate transcriptional repression.
source: While CAMTAs were initially characterized as transcriptional activators, they have also been shown to mediate transcriptional repression (Du et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: CAMT-1 can inhibit CaM expression when available CaM levels are high, by a feedback loop in which CaM regulates its own transcription by binding to IQ domains of CAMT-1.
source: Our data suggest CAMT-1 not only promotes CaM expression in C. elegans neurons, but can also inhibit it when available CaM levels are high, by a feedback loop in which CaM regulates its own transcription by binding to IQ domains of CAMT-1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: CAMT-1 can play a homeostatic role in regulating CaM levels.
source: These data suggest CAMT-1 can play a homeostatic role in regulating CaM levels (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the negative feedback data

claim: Mutant analyses in plants and flies have suggested that CaM binding regulates CAMTA activity.
source: Mutant analyses in plants and flies have already suggested that CaM binding regulates CAMTA activity (Du et al., 2009; Nie et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Binding to CaM converts CAMT-1 from an activator to a repressor.
source: Our data suggest that binding to CaM converts CAMT-1 from an activator to a repressor.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data

claim: Native CaM levels may not be high enough in the circuits studied to evoke negative feedback regulation of CaM expression.
source: The absence of an obvious behavioral phenotype in mutant animals in which CAMT-1's four IQ motifs have been disrupted suggests that native CaM levels may simply not be high enough in the circuits we have studied to evoke negative feedback regulation of CaM expression.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of phenotype in IQ mutants

claim: CAMTA is a general and conserved mechanism by which neurons control levels of CaM.
source: In summary, our data suggest that we have discovered a general and conserved mechanism by which neurons control levels of CaM using CAMTA, a transcription factor that is expressed broadly in the nervous system across Metazoa.
evidence: Inferred from the data across multiple species

claim: Toggling CAMT-1 up and down can change neural excitability, circuit function, and behavior.
source: Toggling CAMT-1, the C. elegans CAMTA, up and down, can change neural excitability, circuit function, and behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The activity of CAMTA transcription factors is regulated in response to upstream signals, and provides a mechanism to alter CaM levels and thereby modulate neural excitability and behavior.
source: We speculate that the activity of CAMTA transcription factors is regulated in response to upstream signals, and provides a mechanism to alter CaM levels and thereby modulate neural excitability and behavior.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the data
